sections.title: Nuclear Radioactivity
objectives: Explain the types of radiation—alpha emission, beta emission, and gamma emission.
Explain the ionization of radiation in an atom.

misconceptions.claim: Alpha radiation is more penetrating than gamma radiation.
misconceptions.correction: Gamma radiation is the most penetrating. Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air, while gamma rays need thick lead or concrete to absorb them.

summary: Some nuclei are radioactive—they spontaneously decay destroying some part of their mass and emitting energetic rays, a process called nuclear radioactivity.
Nuclear radiation, like x rays, is ionizing radiation, because energy sufficient to ionize matter is emitted in each decay.

The range (or distance traveled in a material) of ionizing radiation is directly related to the charge of the emitted particle and its energy, with greater-charge and lower-energy particles having the shortest ranges.

authored_exercises.stem: Name the three main types of nuclear radiation.
authored_exercises.answer: Alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.
solution: Alpha particles are helium nuclei.
Beta particles are fast electrons or positrons.
Gamma rays are high-energy photons.

authored_exercises.stem: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most penetrating?
solution: Alpha particles are stopped by paper.
Beta particles are stopped by a few millimetres of metal.
Gamma rays need thick lead or concrete, so they penetrate most.

authored_exercises.stem: What happens to the atomic number of a nucleus when it emits an alpha particle?
solution: An alpha particle contains two protons and two neutrons.
Losing two protons reduces the atomic number by 2.
The mass number falls by 4.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on Nuclear Radioactivity has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

sections.title: Radiation Detection and Detectors
objectives: Explain the working principle of a Geiger tube.

misconceptions.claim: The clicks from a Geiger counter are the radiation itself.
misconceptions.correction: The clicks are electrical pulses produced when radiation ionizes the gas in the tube. The counter detects the radiation; it does not manufacture or amplify the radiation.

summary: Radiation detectors are based directly or indirectly upon the ionization created by radiation, as are the effects of radiation on living and inert materials.
Explain nuclear radiation.
Explain the types of radiation—alpha emission, beta emission, and gamma emission.

authored_exercises.stem: What is the purpose of a radiation detector?
authored_exercises.answer: To detect and measure ionizing radiation and its intensity.
solution: Radiation ionizes matter along its path.
A detector converts that ionization into a measurable signal.
The signal can show the presence, type and intensity of the radiation.

authored_exercises.stem: Why is a Geiger–Müller tube filled with a gas at low pressure?
authored_exercises.answer: So that incoming radiation can ionize the gas and produce an avalanche of charge that is easily detected.
solution: A high voltage is applied between the central wire and the tube wall.
An ionizing particle starts a cascade of ion pairs.
The avalanche produces a measurable current pulse.

authored_exercises.stem: Why does a Geiger–Müller tube need a thin window at its end?
authored_exercises.answer: So that alpha and low-energy beta particles, which cannot pass through solid walls, can enter the tube.
solution: Alpha particles have a very short range in matter.
A normal metal wall would stop them before they reach the gas.
A thin mica or plastic window lets them through with little energy loss.

sections.title: Substructure of the Nucleus
objectives: Define and discuss the nucleus in an atom.
Calculate the density of the nucleus.

misconceptions.claim: The activity of a radioactive sample stays constant as time passes.
misconceptions.correction: The activity falls exponentially as the nuclei decay. A = λN, so as N decreases the activity decreases with the same half-life as the number of nuclei.

summary: Two particles, both called nucleons, are found inside nuclei. The two types of nucleons are protons and neutrons; they are very similar, except that the proton is positively charged while the neutron is neutral. Some of their characteristics are given in and compared with those of the electron. A mass unit convenient to atomic and nuclear processes is the unified atomic mass unit (u), defined to be 1 u = 1.6605 × 10 − 27 kg = 931.46 MeV / c 2 .

A nuclide is a specific combination of protons and neutrons, denoted by ZAXN or simplyAX,Z is the number of protons or atomic number, X is the symbol for the element, N is the number of neutrons, and A is the mass number or the total number of protons and neutrons, A=N+Z.
Nuclides having the same Z but different N are isotopes of the same element.

sections.title: Nuclear Decay and Conservation Laws
objectives: Calculate the energy emitted during nuclear decay.

misconceptions.claim: In alpha decay the nucleus emits an electron.
misconceptions.correction: It emits a helium nucleus, made of two protons and two neutrons, and the atomic number falls by two. The electron is the beta particle, emitted in beta decay instead.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the electron as an option.

summary: When a parent nucleus decays, it produces a daughter nucleus following rules and conservation laws. There are three major types of nuclear decay, called alpha α, beta β, and gamma γ. The α decay equation is ZAXN→Z−2A−4YN−2+24He2.
Nuclear decay releases an amount of energy E related to the mass destroyed Δm byE=(Δm)c2.
There are three forms of beta decay. The β−decay equation is ZAXN→Z+1AYN−1+β−+ν¯e.

sections.title: Half-Life and Activity
objectives: Calculate age of old objects by radioactive dating.

misconceptions.claim: The half-life of a radioactive sample is the time in which all of it decays.
misconceptions.correction: It is the time in which half the nuclei decay. The sample never decays completely in a finite time, and the same half-life applies however much you start with.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the full decay as an option.

summary: Half-life t1/2 is the time in which there is a 50% chance that a nucleus will decay. The number of nuclei N as a function of time isN=N0e−λt, where N0 is the number present at t=0, and λ is the decay constant, related to the half-life by λ=0.693t1/2.

One of the applications of radioactive decay is radioactive dating, in which the age of a material is determined by the amount of radioactive decay that occurs. The rate of decay is called the activity R:R= Δ N Δ t .
The SI unit for R is the becquerel (Bq), defined by 1 Bq=1 decay/s.

sections.title: Binding Energy
objectives: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of a particle.

misconceptions.claim: A nucleus with more nucleons always has more binding energy per nucleon.
misconceptions.correction: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56. Very light nuclei gain energy by fusion and very heavy nuclei gain energy by fission, so both ends of the curve have lower binding energy per nucleon.

summary: The binding energy (BE) of a nucleus is the energy needed to separate it into individual protons and neutrons. In terms of atomic masses, BE={[Zm(1H)+Nmn]−m(AX)}c2, where m1H is the mass of a hydrogen atom, mAX is the atomic mass of the nuclide, and mn is the mass of a neutron. Patterns in the binding energy per nucleon, BE/A, reveal details of the nuclear force. The larger the BE/A, the more stable the nucleus.
Explain nuclear radiation.
Explain the types of radiation—alpha emission, beta emission, and gamma emission.

sections.title: Tunneling

misconceptions.claim: A particle can tunnel through a potential barrier only if its energy is greater than the barrier height.
misconceptions.correction: Quantum tunneling allows a particle with less energy than the barrier to appear on the other side with a small probability. The probability falls as the barrier gets wider or higher.

summary: Tunneling is a quantum mechanical process of potential energy barrier penetration. The concept was first applied to explain α decay, but tunneling is found to occur in other quantum mechanical systems.
Explain nuclear radiation.
Explain the types of radiation—alpha emission, beta emission, and gamma emission.

sec-7:exr-57.stem: The purpose of this problem is to show in three ways that the binding energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom is negligible compared with the masses of the proton and electron. Use these data: the binding energy of the electron in hydrogen is 13.6 eV; the mass of a hydrogen atom is 1.007825 u; the mass of a proton is 1.007276 u; the mass of an electron is 0.000549 u; and $1\ \mathrm{u}=931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$. (a) Calculate the mass equivalent in u of the 13.6 eV binding energy and compare it with the mass of the hydrogen atom. (b) Subtract the mass of the proton from the mass of the hydrogen atom and show that the difference equals the electron mass to three digits, implying that the binding energy is small. (c) Take the ratio of the binding energy (13.6 eV) to the energy equivalent of the electron mass (0.511 MeV). (d) Discuss how your answers confirm the purpose of the problem.
solution: (a) $m=E/c^{2}=13.6\ \mathrm{eV}/(931.5\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV/u})=1.46\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{u}$, about $10^{-8}$ of the hydrogen atom's mass.
(b) $1.007825\ \mathrm{u}-1.007276\ \mathrm{u}=0.000549\ \mathrm{u}$, which is the electron mass to three digits.
(d) The binding energy changes the mass by about one part in $10^{8}$ of the atom and one part in $10^{5}$ of the electron, so it can be neglected in ordinary mass calculations.

sec-7:exr-41.stem: ${}^{2}H$ is a loosely bound isotope of hydrogen. Called deuterium or heavy hydrogen, it is stable but relatively rare - it is 0.015% of natural hydrogen. Note that deuterium has $Z=N$, which should tend to make it more tightly bound, but both are odd numbers. Calculate $BE/A$, the binding energy per nucleon, for ${}^{2}H$ and compare it with the approximate value of 1.1 MeV per nucleon from the binding-energy curve.
sec-7:exr-41.answer: 1.112 MeV per nucleon, consistent with the approximate curve value of 1.1 MeV per nucleon
solution: The deuteron contains one proton and one neutron. Their masses sum to $1.007276+1.008665=2.015941\ \mathrm{u}$.
The deuteron mass is $2.013553\ \mathrm{u}$, so the mass defect is $2.015941-2.013553=0.002388\ \mathrm{u}$.
The binding energy is $(0.002388)(931.5)=2.224\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and $BE/A=2.224/2=1.112\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon.
This agrees with the approximate value of 1.1 MeV per nucleon read from the binding-energy curve.
